newsitem.title: CANADA: NBA-ISIAH THOMAS TO BECOME TORONTO RAPTORS OWNER.
newsitem.headline: NBA-ISIAH THOMAS TO BECOME TORONTO RAPTORS OWNER.

text.p: Toronto Raptors general manager and former NBA star Isiah Thomas is set to become the first African-American to be majority owner of a major league sports team in North America.

The 36-year-old Thomas signed a letter of intent to buy controlling interest of the second-year Raptors and said Tuesday that Canada's amenable racial climate helped pave the way for his historic rise to the owners' box.
"From a racial standpoint...what I've found to be true in the (United) States is not necessarily true here in Canada," Thomas told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

"Whereas race sometimes can stop you from getting the job in the United States, I haven't found that to be the case here," said Thomas, who as a player led the Detroit Pistons to two National Basketball Association titles.
Before Thomas officially takes over as Raptors owner, the final transfer of the team must be approved by the NBA board of governors.

Thomas and his group of U.S. and Canadian investors negotiated the final aspects of the deal Monday night with majority owner Allan Slaight, who currently holds 81 percent of the club. Under the deal, Slaight will retain a minority interest in the team.
The agreement headed off a potential mutiny of top players on the Toronto squad.

Thomas had threatened to sell his nine percent interest in the team and quit as general manager if the deal did not go through. Raptors star guard Damon Stoudamire told reporters that he would seek a trade if the popular Thomas left the club and suggested some of his teammates would follow.

Under Thomas's guidance, the Raptors finished with a 30-52 record this season -- last place in the Central Division but a nine-victory improvement over their inaugural season. Toronto had a better record than eight other NBA teams and posted 16 more wins than the Vancouver Grizzlies, who joined the league the same season as the Raptors.

Thomas's historic purchase of the Raptors comes on the heels of Tiger Woods becoming the first African-American to win one of golf's majors at the Masters earlier this month, and the decision by Major League Baseball to retire Jackie Robinson's jersey number to honour the man who broke baseball's colour line 50 years ago this month.
Toronto Blue Jays manager Cito Gaston, the first black manager to win the World Series, complained last week that some of his critics in the Toronto media were racists.
But in the afterglow of the Raptors' deal, Thomas seemed intent on promoting his belief in Canada's superior racial attitudes over a drink with Gaston.
"Cito and I will go out and have a beer," Thomas told the Toronto Star newspaper.
